name: Secure Computation (MPC, FHE, ZK)
description: Secure multiparty computation, homomorphic encryption, zero-knowledge proofs, and private set operations.

uss.narrative:
The earliest USENIX Security entries here mark the moment secure computation pivoted from theory toward deployable systems. GAZELLE (USENIX 2018) showed that combining homomorphic encryption with garbled circuits could make secure neural network inference practical, while DIZK (USENIX 2018) attacked the scalability of zero-knowledge proofs by distributing SNARK generation across a cluster. Mobile Private Contact Discovery at Scale (USENIX 2019) carried the same systems-engineering spirit into private set intersection, turning a privacy-preserving primitive into something a messaging app could actually run against millions of contacts.

Around 2020-2021 the area broadened from raw primitives to real-world applications and reusable building blocks. Secure Multi-party Computation of Differentially Private Median (USENIX 2020) and Secure parallel computation on national scale volumes of data (USENIX 2020) pushed MPC toward statistics and graph workloads at scale, while DatashareNetwork (USENIX 2020) and Identifying Harmful Media in End-to-End Encrypted Communication (USENIX 2021) applied private search and membership testing to journalism and abuse detection. Poseidon (USENIX 2021) was a quiet but pivotal shift: by designing a hash function native to ZK arithmetic circuits, it became core infrastructure for the SNARK/STARK ecosystem. GForce (USENIX 2021) and Fuzzy Labeled PSI (USENIX 2021) meanwhile extended privacy-preserving inference to GPUs and biometric search.

By 2022-2023 the work matured along several distinct threads. Private set operations diversified into union, cardinality, and multi-party variants, with Linear Private Set Union (USENIX 2023) and Efficient Unbalanced PSI Cardinality (USENIX 2023) improving asymptotics and contact-tracing use cases, and Estimating Incidental Collection in Foreign Intelligence Surveillance (USENIX 2022) applying large-scale multiparty PSI to surveillance auditing. FHE became a systems-optimization target in its own right with ELASM (USENIX 2023) managing error-latency tradeoffs in CKKS-style schemes. ZK proofs moved toward concrete impact, with Cheesecloth (USENIX 2023) proving real-world vulnerabilities in zero knowledge and Eos (USENIX 2023) enabling private delegation of expensive zkSNARK provers, while GigaDORAM (USENIX 2023) broke the billion-address barrier for oblivious RAM.

The 2024 cohort shows a field that is both deeply specialized and increasingly fused with machine learning. A cluster of papers - Scalable MPC Protocols for ML in the Honest-Majority Setting, MD-ML, OblivGNN, and Scalable Zero-knowledge Proofs for Non-linear Functions in Machine Learning - target privacy-preserving and verifiable ML across threat models and architectures. FHE saw both attacks and engineering advances, with Key Recovery Attacks on Approximate Homomorphic Encryption (USENIX 2024) exposing weaknesses in noise-flooding defenses and DaCapo (USENIX 2024) automating bootstrapping management. Polynomial-commitment and secret-sharing machinery (Fast RS-IOP Multivariate Polynomial Commitments, USENIX 2024), verifiable aggregation (PINE, USENIX 2024), distributed PRFs (LaKey, USENIX 2024), and multi-party PSI (O-Ring and K-Star, USENIX 2024) round out a landscape that has moved decisively from "can we do this securely" to "how do we do it at scale, robustly, and with verified correctness."

ndss.narrative:
The earliest work in this set, all from NDSS 2020, was dominated by the race to make privacy-preserving machine learning practical through custom multiparty computation frameworks. "Trident: Efficient 4PC Framework for Privacy Preserving Machine Learning" (NDSS 2020) and "BLAZE: Blazing Fast Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning" (NDSS 2020) pushed small-party (3PC/4PC) protocols toward usable training and inference speeds, while "MACAO: A Maliciously-Secure and Client-Efficient Active ORAM Framework" (NDSS 2020) and "Secure Sublinear Time Differentially Private Median Computation" (NDSS 2020) showed the same community attacking oblivious data access and private analytics. The common theme was clear: MPC was moving from asymptotic theory toward engineered systems.

Over the next few years the field broadened along two axes. On the ML side, "GALA: Greedy ComputAtion for Linear Algebra in Privacy-Preserved Neural Networks" (NDSS 2021) attacked the linear-algebra bottleneck in private inference, "POSEIDON: Privacy-Preserving Federated Neural Network Learning" (NDSS 2021) brought FHE to federated training, and "Tetrad: Actively Secure 4PC for Secure Training and Inference" (NDSS 2022) continued the 4PC lineage begun by Trident. Meanwhile the trust model itself became a design knob: "Hybrid Trust Multi-party Computation with Trusted Execution Environment" (NDSS 2022) blended SGX hardware with cryptographic MPC. Alongside this, a distinct zero-knowledge and distributed-cryptography thread matured through "Transparency Dictionaries with Succinct Proofs of Correct Operation" (NDSS 2022) and "hbACSS: How to Robustly Share Many Secrets" (NDSS 2022), and FHE-based inference reached striking speeds in "REDsec: Running Encrypted Discretized Neural Networks in Seconds" (NDSS 2023).

By 2024–2025 the area visibly matured from bespoke protocols into tooling, compilers, and testing. "HEIR: A Unified Representation for Cross-Scheme Compilation of Fully Homomorphic Computation" (NDSS 2024) treated FHE as a compilation target, while "MPCDiff: Testing and Repairing MPC-Hardened Deep Learning Models" (NDSS 2024) and "MTZK: Testing and Exploring Bugs in Zero-Knowledge (ZK) Compilers" (NDSS 2025) signaled that the ecosystem was large enough to need its own debugging infrastructure. At the same time, the ML target grew from small networks to transformers: "SHAFT: Secure, Handy, Accurate and Fast Transformer Inference" (NDSS 2025) made encrypted transformer inference a first-class goal, and "Pencil: Private and Extensible Collaborative Learning without the Non-Colluding Assumption" (NDSS 2024) chipped away at the standard non-colluding assumption. Private set operations also kept advancing, from "Faster Secure Comparisons with Offline Phase for Efficient Private Set Intersection" (NDSS 2023) to "Recurrent Private Set Intersection for Unbalanced Databases with Cuckoo Hashing and Leveled FHE" (NDSS 2025).

The most recent work, from NDSS 2026, shows the area converging on production-scale LLM privacy, verifiability, and ever-leaner primitives. "STIP: Three-Party Privacy-Preserving and Lossless Inference for Large Transformers in Production" (NDSS 2026) targets deployed large-transformer services, "CRISP: An Efficient Cryptographic Framework for ML Inference Against Malicious Clients" (NDSS 2026) hardens inference beyond the semi-honest model, and "VeriLoRA: Fine-Tuning Large Language Models with Verifiable Security via Zero-Knowledge Proofs" (NDSS 2026) fuses ZK proofs with LLM fine-tuning to guarantee correctness. Systems concerns like bandwidth now drive design in "RoundRole: Unlocking the Efficiency of Multi-party Computation with Bandwidth-aware Execution" (NDSS 2026), while private set operations keep splitting into specialized variants such as "cwPSU: Efficient Unbalanced Private Set Union via Constant-weight Codes" (NDSS 2026) and "Faster Than Ever: A New Lightweight Private Set Intersection and Its Variants" (NDSS 2026). In short, the area has traveled from proving that private neural-network inference was feasible at all to deploying private, verifiable, and accountable computation over the largest models in production.

sp.narrative:
The earliest work in this slice, all from IEEE S&P 2018, laid the cryptographic groundwork that the next decade would build on. Bulletproofs (S&P 2018) delivered short, transparent zero-knowledge range proofs with no trusted setup and was quickly adopted for confidential blockchain transactions, while Doubly-Efficient zkSNARKs Without Trusted Setup (S&P 2018) attacked the same trusted-setup problem for general NP statements. Alongside proofs, the period produced practical building blocks: Secure Two-party Threshold ECDSA from ECDSA Assumptions (S&P 2018) and frameworks like xJsnark and vRAM that made verifiable computation over programs and RAM concrete rather than theoretical.

Around 2019-2020 the emphasis shifted from primitives to systems and usability. SoK: General Purpose Compilers for Secure Multi-Party Computation (S&P 2019) mapped the crowded MPC compiler landscape, and New Primitives for Actively-Secure MPC over Rings (S&P 2019) pushed efficient malicious security toward machine-learning workloads. That machine-learning pull became the dominant theme: CrypTFlow (S&P 2020) automatically compiled TensorFlow inference into MPC, Helen (S&P 2019) handled maliciously secure collaborative linear models, and ZEXE (S&P 2020) extended the zero-knowledge line into decentralized private smart-contract computation. Transparent Polynomial Delegation (S&P 2020) and Efficient and Secure Multiparty Computation from Fixed-Key Block Ciphers (S&P 2020) kept sharpening the underlying proof and garbling machinery.

The 2021-2024 stretch is where secure computation became genuinely fast and specialized. Wolverine (S&P 2021) scaled VOLE-based zero-knowledge to huge circuits, CryptGPU (S&P 2021) and Orca (S&P 2024) moved private ML onto GPUs, and SiRnn (S&P 2021), SecFloat (S&P 2022), and BOLT (S&P 2024) chased accurate secure evaluation of the messy nonlinear functions in RNNs, floating point, and transformers. FHE matured in parallel through PEGASUS (S&P 2021) and the SoK: Fully Homomorphic Encryption Compilers (S&P 2021), while CirC (S&P 2022) unified proof systems, MPC, and FHE behind common compiler infrastructure. A distinct federated-learning cluster also emerged, with ELSA, RoFL, and Flamingo (all S&P 2023) hardening secure aggregation against malicious clients.

The most recent work, at S&P 2026, shows the area consolidating around scalable proofs, encrypted computation at database scale, and adversarial scrutiny. Zero-knowledge is trending toward folding-based and distributed provers in Nebula: Proving Machine Executions via Folding Schemes, Coral's succinct CFG proofs, Pianist-style distribution continued in Single-Server Private Outsourcing of zk-SNARKs, while FHE reaches for real query workloads in APEX: Accurate Parallel Expressive Homomorphic Execution for Encrypted Databases. Private set and correlation machinery advances through Practical Multi-Party Private Set Intersection with Reducible Zero-Sharing and Dory: Streaming PCG with Small Memory, and private smart contracts continue with Jigsaw: Doubly Private Smart Contracts. Tellingly, the field is now auditing its own deployments: the Hollow-LLM Attack (S&P 2026) exposes computationally trivial weights that break zero-knowledge verification of LLM inference, a sign that secure computation for machine learning is mature enough to be attacked, not just proposed.

ccs.narrative:
Secure multiparty computation, homomorphic encryption, and zero-knowledge proofs form one of the largest and most technically active threads at CCS. The 2018 cohort established the landscape: ABY3: A Mixed Protocol Framework for Machine Learning (CCS 2018) combined secret-sharing arithmetic and boolean circuits in a three-party model tailored for ML, while Compressing Vector OLE (CCS 2018) introduced compression techniques for the correlation-generation building blocks underlying modern MPC. Simultaneously, ALCHEMY: A Language and Compiler for Homomorphic Encryption Made easY (CCS 2018) lowered the barrier to writing FHE programs.

The 2019-2020 era pushed MPC into neural network training. QUOTIENT: Two-Party Secure Neural Network Training and Prediction (CCS 2019) showed that training, not just inference, was feasible under two-party computation, and Asynchronous Distributed Key Generation for Computationally-Secure Randomness, Consensus, and Threshold Signatures (CCS 2020) addressed the setup problem for threshold cryptography at scale. Zero-knowledge IOPs gained traction with Ligero++: A New Optimized Sublinear IOP (CCS 2020), removing the trusted-setup dependency entirely.

By 2022-2024, the field reached production systems. Reinforced Concrete: A Fast Hash Function for Verifiable Computation (CCS 2022) co-designed a hash for both ZK prover efficiency and native speed. EIFFeL: Ensuring Integrity for Federated Learning (CCS 2022) married secure aggregation with integrity guarantees. Chaghri - A FHE-friendly Block Cipher (CCS 2022) demonstrated that symmetric primitives could be re-engineered for FHE evaluation. zkLLM: Zero Knowledge Proofs for Large Language Models (CCS 2024) capped the timeline by proving correct LLM inference with ZK.

milestones.note: Compressed the correlation-generation phase of MPC, substantially reducing communication overhead for VOLE-based protocols.

milestones.title: zkLLM: Zero Knowledge Proofs for Large Language Models
milestones.note: Produced ZK proofs for billion-parameter LLM inference, demonstrating verifiable AI at unprecedented scale.

top4.narrative:
The earliest work here, all from 2018, split along two lines that would define the decade. On the proof side, Bulletproofs (S&P 2018) delivered very short zero-knowledge range proofs with no trusted setup, while Doubly-Efficient zkSNARKs Without Trusted Setup (S&P 2018), xJsnark (S&P 2018), and the distributed prover of DIZK (USENIX 2018) attacked the practicality of general verifiable computation. On the secure-computation side, GAZELLE (USENIX 2018) combined homomorphic encryption with garbled circuits for fast private neural-network inference, Secure Outsourced Matrix Computation (CCS 2018) pushed FHE toward the same goal, and a cluster of threshold-ECDSA papers (Fast Multiparty Threshold ECDSA, Fast Secure Multiparty ECDSA, and Secure Two-party Threshold ECDSA, all 2018) chased cryptocurrency key custody. Compressing Vector OLE (CCS 2018) quietly introduced a building block — cheap correlated randomness — that later systems would lean on heavily.

Between 2019 and 2021 the field matured into engineering. Secure machine learning became the dominant application: QUOTIENT (CCS 2019) tackled training, while CrypTFlow (S&P 2020), CryptGPU (S&P 2021), SiRnn (S&P 2021), and Helen (S&P 2019) scaled private inference toward real models and hardware, and New Primitives for Actively-Secure MPC over Rings (S&P 2019) hardened the underlying protocols against malicious parties. Two SoKs — on general-purpose MPC compilers (S&P 2019) and FHE compilers (S&P 2021) — signaled that usability, not just feasibility, was now the question. Zero-knowledge kept accelerating in parallel: Transparent Polynomial Delegation (S&P 2020) and Wolverine (S&P 2021) drove down cost and removed trusted setup, and Poseidon (USENIX 2021) fixed the hashing bottleneck that had throttled SNARK circuits. FHE gained expressiveness through PEGASUS (S&P 2021), and private analytics appeared with Lightweight Techniques for Private Heavy Hitters (S&P 2021).

By 2022–2024 the emphasis shifted to deployed applications and to defending collaborative learning. ZEXE (S&P 2020) and zk-creds (S&P 2023) turned succinct proofs into private computation and anonymous credentials, and zkBridge (CCS 2022) used them to build trustless cross-chain bridges. Federated learning became a battleground for integrity and robustness — EIFFeL (CCS 2022), ELSA (S&P 2023), and RoFL (S&P 2023) all worked to keep malicious clients from poisoning securely aggregated models. BOLT (S&P 2024) then carried efficient private inference into the transformer era.

The most recent work, concentrated at NDSS 2026, shows a field that is both broadening and specializing. Efficiency remains central — RoundRole squeezes MPC throughput with bandwidth-aware execution, and VDORAM builds a RAM that is at once publicly verifiable and distributedly oblivious. Private set operations are being re-optimized in Faster Than Ever (PSI) and cwPSU (unbalanced private set union), while FHE powers cross-dataset analytics in Select-Then-Compute. Secure ML inference is being pushed to full malicious security in CRISP, and secure aggregation gains accountability in WhiteCloak. Auctions get dedicated treatment in Cryptobazaar and Scalable Off-Chain Auctions. Capping the arc, VeriLoRA applies zero-knowledge proofs to verifiable LLM fine-tuning — closing the loop from 2018's foundational proof systems to today's demand for privacy and verifiability inside large-scale AI.
